title: subword-prefetch-scheduling-kernel-compatibility-protocol
content:
Summary:

This note proposes a lightweight protocol and runtime changes to coordinate subword (tokenization) prefetching across the serving runtime, the scheduler, and kernel selection layers. The goal is to reduce end-to-end tokenization latency for short/medium inputs and avoid duplicate tokenization work when requests are batched or partial-prefetches are served from KV cache.

Motivation and pain points observed:
- High p50 latency for chat-like short prompts where tokenization-O(1) overhead is non-trivial relative to model time (esp for trimmed/quantized kernels).
- Duplicate tokenization CPU cycles when a batch contains many requests with overlapping prefixes (e.g., system prompt + user prompt templates).
- Mismatch between token boundaries expected by some optimized kernels (subword-aligned input) and naive byte-level prefetchers leading to misaligned KV cache hits and extra work.
- Backpressure interactions where tokenization stalls the GPU scheduling path for small batches; current runtime treats tokenization as synchronous pre-step.

Goals and non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Define a protocol between tokenizer worker(s), scheduler, and kernel compatibility layer to allow:
    - speculative/partial subword prefetch for hot prefixes
    - compatibility hints for kernels about required alignment or padding
    - KV-cache keys that are stable across prefetch variants
  - Reduce redundant work for overlapping prefixes in micro-batches while keeping latency predictable.
  - Maintain graceful degradation: if prefetch fails or cache misses, fallback to synchronous tokenization with bounded added latency.
- Non-goals:
  - Replace model-level tokenization; this is an infrastructure/runtime optimization only.
  - Complex full-NLP cache (we are not designing a semantic dedup system).

Design overview (high level):
- Introduce a Subword Prefetch Protocol (SPP) that exposes three primitives: HINT, PREFETCH, BIND.
  - HINT: lightweight metadata attached to a request describing likely prefix tokens (or prefix hash) and kernel alignment requirements. HINT is issued at ingress before full text is available to tokenizer workers in some cases (e.g., known system prompt).
  - PREFETCH: request to tokenizer pool to produce a partial encoding up to N subwords (or up to a boundary) and materialize a stable cache key for prefix. The tokenizer may emit both raw subword ids and an alignment token (chainable boundary marker).
  - BIND: binder step used by scheduler to associate a serving request with an existing prefetched entry (cache hit) and to claim ownership so further PREFETCHes don't duplicate work.

Details and rationale for each primitive:
- HINT semantics:
  - Small JSON blob: {prefix_id, approx_length_chars, alignment_profile}. prefix_id is a stable hash computed by the caller (e.g., MD5 of system prompt) so different requests with same system prompt can be deduped at scheduler. alignment_profile is one of {ANY, SUBWORD_SAFE, PAD_16, PAD_32} describing kernel preferences.
  - HINTs are optional. In hosted flows we populate HINT with common templates (system prompt, assistant persona) at the API ingress layer.
- PREFETCH behavior and outputs:
  - Tokenizer worker returns: {prefetch_id, token_ids_base64, length_tokens, canonical_key}. canonical_key is what we store in the KV prefix cache and is computed deterministically from prefix_id + alignment_profile + tokenization settings (vocab, normalization flags).
  - Prefetches can be partial (first K tokens) where K is selected from a small set (K in {8,16,32}). We choose K based on observed prefix length distribution and downstream kernel startup costs.
  - Prefetch should be cancellable and revocable; workers expose a cancel token so scheduler can avoid waiting for long tokenizations for low-priority requests.
- BIND and ownership:
  - Scheduler receives prefetched canonical_key and tries to bind incoming requests that match the HINT/prefix_id. Binding is the atomic claim preventing multiple scheduler threads from issuing duplicate PREFETCH calls for the same prefix.
  - If BIND finds an in-progress prefetch, it can either attach to the in-flight future or issue a prioritized duplicate only if binding fails within a timeout (5–10ms).

Scheduler integration and prioritization rules:
- New Priority class: TOKENIZATION_PREP (higher than background but lower than GPU_READY).
- When a request arrives with a HINT and matching canonical_key in prefix index, scheduler attempts immediate BIND; if bound to a cold cache entry it will schedule PREFETCH on tokenizer pool before assigning to a GPU slot.
- Prefetches are charged to a separate CPU budget; scheduling must ensure long-running prefetches cannot exhaust CPU resources and starve critical network/io tasks. Config knobs: max-prefetch-per-worker, total-prefetch-concurrency, per-customer-prefetch-rate.
- For micro-batching: when a batch is formed, scheduler should attempt to coalesce BINDs with overlapping canonical_keys and enumerate a minimal prefetch set for the batch. E.g., 24 requests with 3 unique canonical_keys => schedule up to 3 PREFETCH tasks instead of 24.

Kernel compatibility / alignment contract:
- Many optimized kernels (fused attention variants, quantized token-interned kernels) expect certain alignment/padding of token buffers for vectorized loads. The alignment_profile from HINT is propagated to tokenizer so prefetch outputs include padding tokens (a special PAD_ID) to meet kernel constraints or a compatibility descriptor describing minimal padding.
- canonical_key must encode alignment_profile so a cached prefix padded for PAD_32 is not accidentally used by a PAD_16 kernel without repadding. We avoid re-tokenizing but allow a cheap repadding step: when a kernel requires stricter padding than cached, runtime uses a lightweight pad-adapter (no re-tokenization) that updates token_id sequence and adjusts metadata.

KV cache interaction and key design:
- Store prefetched encodings in the KV prefix cache under canonical_key. Canonical_key = hash(prefix_id || tokenizer_version || alignment_profile || normalization_flags). This ensures deterministic lookup.
- Cache entries contain: token_ids (base64), token_count, last_used_ts, producer_version. We avoid storing original text to keep cache small and to reduce PII risk.
- Eviction policy: LRU with weight by token_count; small prefixes are cheap and should be kept longer per unit memory. Provide eviction hints from scheduler when a particular prefix is dominant for an active GPU pool.
- On cache hit, scheduler BIND returns token_ids and the request execution can skip tokenizer worker entirely and proceed to KV-cache -> GPU path.

Fallbacks and correctness:
- If a kernel requires exact tokenization (rare), then PREFETCH is advisory; BIND will verify token_count and run full synchronous tokenization before model input if mismatch.
- For correctness, the runtime must preserve tokenizer configuration fingerprint (tokenizer_version) as part of the cache key and serve routes. Any model rollout that updates tokenizer config invalidates relevant canonical_keys. Rollout plan must include cache flush or versioned canonical_keys.

Microbenchmarks and measurement plan:
- Bench goals: reduce tokenization p50 by 20–40ms on short prompts; reduce CPU tokenization cycles per-request by 30% for common prefixes; measure GPU idle time waiting for tokenization.
- Bench setup: synthetic workload with 60% repeated system prompt, 30% templated user messages, 10% unique long messages. Measure with K=8/16/32 prefetch sizes and alignment_profile variations.
- Instrumentation: add spans around HINT->PREFETCH->BIND in trace traces, expose per-request tokenization_time, prefetch_wait_time, and cache_hit boolean to Console.

Rollout strategy:
- Phase 0: feature flag at runtime level, tokenizer pool-only (no scheduler coalescing). Pilot on non-critical tenants.
- Phase 1: enable scheduler BIND coalescing and KV prefix cache writes. Monitor tokenization CPU, latency SLOs, and memory footprint.
- Phase 2: enable alignment hints to kernels and pad-adapter optimizations. Collect kernel mismatch stats and refine alignment_profile taxonomy.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- Prefetch sizing: static K buckets are simple but may be suboptimal; can we infer optimal K from request histogram per-tenant? Cost: increased complexity and more metadata.
- Security/PII: we purposely avoid storing original text in the prefix cache; what about deduping by prefix_id collisions? Use long hashes and tenant-scoped salts.
- Cross-tenant prefix sharing: useful for saving work but dangerous for privacy/compliance. Default: prefix_id is tenant-scoped; optional global sharing behind enterprise consent.
- Cache coherence on tokenizer model updates: how aggressive should automatic invalidation be? Prefer explicit rollout-triggered invalidation.

Next steps / TODOs:
- Prototype PREFETCH/BIND RPC in tokenizer-pool service (API stub + mock kernel). Owner: Diego. ETA: 3 weeks.
- Implement canonical_key computation library shared between ingress and tokenizer workers. Owner: Evan. ETA: 2 weeks.
- Add telemetry spans and metrics for prefetch-hit-rate, prefetch-latency, prefetch-cancel-rate. Owner: Maya. ETA: 1 week.
- Write benchmark harness and run on internal micro-cluster. Owner: Priya. ETA: 3 weeks.

Appendix: example flows
1) Common system prompt flow (fast path):
  - Ingress attaches HINT {prefix_id=hash(system), alignment_profile=PAD_16}
  - Scheduler sees existing canonical_key in prefix index (cache hit) => BIND -> attach token_ids -> send to GPU
  - Result: tokenization time for request ~0ms.
2) New template during heavy traffic (coalesce):
  - 50 concurrent requests with same HINT arrive. Scheduler receives 50 events, detects 1 unique canonical_key -> issues 1 PREFETCH to tokenizer pool, others attach to in-flight future. When prefetch completes, all 50 BIND and proceed, saving 49 tokenizations.

References and related notes:
- See related RFC: RFC-2024-07-subword-prefetch (design rationale, simulation results)
- Related PRs on GitHub: runtime/pull/482 (tokenizer pool hooks), runtime/pull/491 (kv-prefix cache schema)
